title: Tristan Luneau's Point Streak Is Real, But Most of It Comes From Long Shots and Power Plays
dek: The Ducks defenseman has 11 points in ten games, and the chance data says part of that is earned and part is a hot stretch.
text:
Tristan Luneau is 22, a right-shot defenseman from Victoriaville, Quebec, and for the last few weeks he has been one of the more productive blueliners in the league. He has 13 points in 19 games for Anaheim, 17th among 206 defensemen. He also has 11 points in his last ten games. The question for a Ducks team sitting at 10-8-1 is how much of that is a new level and how much is a streak.

## Who he is

Anaheim took Luneau 53rd overall in the second round of 2022, out of the Gatineau Olympiques of the QMJHL. Central Scouting's final ranking had him No. 24 among North American skaters, and No. 10 at midterm, so he went later than the scouts' own list suggested.

The junior résumé shows steady growth. He had 18 points in 31 games in 2020-21, then 43 in 63 the next year, then 83 points (20 goals) in 65 games in 2022-23. Our league translation, which converts junior scoring into what it would be worth over an 82-game NHL season, puts that last year at about 29 points. That is a strong number for a defenseman and it shows where the offense comes from: he moves the puck and joins the play.

The data we have doesn't include his international record or how the players drafted around him have done, so we'll leave those out.

His NHL path has been gradual. He had 14 games and four points before this season, including one game last season. This is not a rookie year by the league's definition, but it is his first real stretch. He now has 33 NHL games and 17 points (6 goals, 11 assists).

## How he's being talked about

The coverage is mostly fantasy and highlights. Yardbarker's headline on November 10 reads "Fantasy Hockey: Kartye, Luneau, Kantserov See Rising Ice Time." CBS Sports ran "Ducks' Tristan Luneau: Riding eight-game point streak" on November 9. NHL.com's recaps are titled "Luneau Finds the Net With Long-Range Shot" and "Luneau finishes slick play."

Those headlines tell us two things. He is producing, and fantasy writers have noticed. One caution: Yardbarker's piece says his ice time is rising, but the game log shows the opposite over this stretch. We'll come back to that.

## What the season looks like

The raw line is 4 goals and 9 assists in 19 games, with 4 of those points on the power play. He averages 20:04 a night, which ranks 86th among 206 defensemen, so he is a regular but not a workhorse. He has 23 shots on goal, 4 hits and 24 blocks.

The last ten games are the hot part: 11 points, 4 of them goals. We'd expect about 4.4 points at his ice time, so he is scoring at roughly two and a half times the pace the model projects. He has also scored 4 goals when the model expected 0.8 over that stretch.

That is where the caution comes in. Expected goals measures the quality of a team's chances, based on where and how shots are taken. Over the full season, Luneau's own shots are worth 1.55 expected goals, and he has scored 4. His goals minus expected is +2.45. His own expected goals rank 65th among 206 defensemen, which is solid but nowhere near his points rank of 17th.

## What is really driving it

**His own chances.** The recent form does include some real improvement. Over the last ten games his shots are worth 1.0 expected goals, against 0.7 that his ice time would normally produce. So he is getting somewhat better looks, though not 4-goals-in-ten-games better.

**Where he shoots from.** He has 41 unblocked shots this season, with an average distance of 48 feet. Only 2 of them came from inside 15 feet (1 goal, 0.3 expected goals) and 2 from 15 to 30 feet (no goals, 0.2 expected). The other 37 came from beyond 30 feet, with 3 goals on 1.1 expected goals. That is a defenseman's shot map: mostly point shots, which rarely go in. The busiest areas confirm it: 6 shots on goal from the right point and 5 from the center point, with no goals from either. His goals came from the high slot (3 shots, 2 goals) and outside right (3 shots, 1 goal). Headlines about a "long-range shot" fit the data, but the volume of long shots is also why his own expected-goals number is modest. Finishing at this rate from distance usually fades.

**Who he plays with.** The team side is the more encouraging part. With Luneau on the ice, Anaheim has 2.75 more goals than expected. His five-on-five share of expected goals is 52.86%, meaning the Ducks create slightly more of the quality chances than they allow while he plays, and the team as a whole sits at 48.6%. The Ducks are also 14.08 percentage points better in expected-goal share with him on the ice than without him. That is a large gap, though over 19 games it needs to be treated loosely.

His ice-time trend also matters. He is playing 19:04 a night over the last ten games, down 2:07 from his earlier average, and his game log shows three straight games between 15:54 and 18:00 in the middle of the streak. His production has come in fewer minutes, which helps explain why the model sees him as more efficient than usual. Whether the coaches trust him with the bigger minutes of early October is something to watch.

## How the model sees him

The model blends this season with last season and his role, because a few weeks of games is too few to trust alone. It rates his own scoring chances at 0.23 expected goals per 60 minutes, which is low, and his on-ice expected goals for at 2.82 per 60, which is better. He gets a point on 45% of the goals scored while he's on the ice, an unusually high share, and the kind that tends to come down.

Evolving-Hockey's value models, which cover earlier seasons, are a useful reminder. In 2023-24 he rated at -0.2 wins above replacement over 7 games, ranked 172nd of 224 defensemen. They also noted he played with weaker teammates (bottom 9%) and against the toughest competition (bottom 2% by their measure), which hurts raw numbers. His defense was the problem: opponents got 0.11 more expected goals per 60 with him on the ice. That sample was small (125 minutes), so it tells us where his defensive game started, not where it is now.

## What to watch next

Three things will tell us whether this is a new level.

First, the shot map. If he gets more shots from the high slot and fewer from the point, the goals become more sustainable. If it stays at 37 of 41 from beyond 30 feet, expect the goals to dry up.

Second, ice time. His 17 points would hold more weight if he regains the 21-minute nights, as in the Buffalo and Nashville games. Sitting at 16 minutes on a hot streak suggests the coaches are managing him.

Third, defense. His recent team numbers (52.86% expected-goal share) are encouraging, but the earlier data flagged chances allowed as his weak spot. A real improvement there would be the most meaningful change.

What would change our view: if the goal rate falls back toward the 0.8 the model expected while his chance creation stays the same, he is a useful, point-producing defenseman. If the chances improve and the production holds, he is more than that.
